cases.rationale: Authors explicitly state an overall replication verdict on the main findings. Their discussion describes external-validity differences as complementing earlier research and the factor modification as minor. New test–retest and expert-rating analyses are extensions. Under the existing author-framing rule, the source supports retaining successful; the earlier proposed mixed correction is withheld from implementation. Blind Sol mixed and blind Opus successful remain preserved, so this is source adjudication, not a claim of two-model agreement.
cases.strongest_opposing_reading: The age/training relation with hyperactivity was null originally and non-null now; four item means differ, and one cross-loading item was removed. A finding-by-finding reading supports mixed. The parent rejects this as a correction under the authors’ explicit overall verdict, while preserving all contrasts.
cases.reviewer_correction: The reviewer summary misnumbers the changed questionnaire items. Its own validated source proof correctly names inattention1,2,12 and hyperactivity6; those literal source numbers govern. No raw reviewer output is edited.

primary_evidence.quote: Comparing V Dog ARS and C Dog ARS data, inattention items 1, 2, and 12 as well as hyperactivity/impulsivity item 6 differed across the datasets (see Table 3 ). The mean scores on inattention items 1, 2, and 12 mean were higher in the current sample whereas the mean score on hyperactivity/impulsivity item 6 was higher in V Dog ARS sample (see Table 3 ).

We replicated the main findings of Vas et al. [ 14 ] in new samples, and our results confirmed the previously obtained factor structure of the questionnaire (inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity) with a minor modification (deletion of item 4 due to cross-loading).

Our findings on external validity, specifically, age-related decrease in owner-rated inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity, effect of training experience, and sex on these factors, complement earlier research. Vas and colleagues found associations between the inattention scale and age and training status, but no associations between hyperactivity/impulsivity and these variables.

Summarizing key aims and results, the current study replicated the factor structure of the Dog ARS, with evidence of good internal consistency and test–retest reliability of inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity subscales, revealed three ambiguous items that may need modification in the future, and for the first time included expert ratings of the Dog ARS, where fair (inattention subscale) to moderate (hyperactivity/impulsivity subscale) agreement was detected between owners and trainers.
